docs.title: KendoDojoManagement
docs.text: Self-hosted web application for managing the members, sessions, and attendance of a kendo dojo. Single-dojo per instance, deployed with rootless Podman.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Members — full profile management with grade history, coach/first-aider flags, and under-18 safeguarding fields
  • Sessions — recurring templates and ad-hoc sessions with per-type colour coding, iCal feed, and a calendar/list toggle view
  • Attendance — self check-in, one shareable check-in link per session, admin overrides, and visitor records
  • Grades — enforced kendo grade progression (Mukyū → 8-dan) with full audit trail
  • Federations — per-member federation memberships with membership numbers and renewal tracking. The catalogue starts empty; add the federations your dojo uses in Admin Settings. The FIK affiliate list is the authoritative source for official names, abbreviations and websites.
  • Reports — attendance and member-grade reports with CSV export
  • Auth — passkey (WebAuthn) primary, recovery codes, admin-issued recovery tokens, and break-glass CLI token
  • Security — rate limiting, account lockout, security headers, CORS, and structured security event logging

docs.title: Container runtime
docs.text:
Podman is the supported runtime. It is what the project is developed and tested against, and what both deployment paths target: rootless, daemonless, systemd-native.

Docker is best-effort and unverified. The Compose files use no Podman-specific syntax and the Makefile auto-detects docker compose, so it is expected to work — but nothing here is tested under Docker and no parity is promised. Bug reports are welcome; behaviour differences are not treated as release blockers.

Every command in these docs is written in its podman / podman-compose form. With the podman-docker shim installed, docker and docker compose are aliases for these, so both spellings work; a clean Podman install has no docker binary at all, which is why the Podman form is the one written out.

Compose files keep their docker-compose.*.yml names — that is the filename Compose implementations look for by convention, and -f names them explicitly at every call site regardless of runtime.

docs.title: Deployment paths
docs.text:
Two supported ways to run this in production — pick one:

Path Files Use when Compose docker-compose.yml + .env You want a single host up quickly. Traefik terminates TLS on 80/443 with a Let's Encrypt certificate over the HTTP challenge. See Quick self-host. Quadlet deploy/quadlet You want the hardened deployment: rootless systemd units, Traefik with automatic TLS, network segmentation, Podman secrets, automated backups. ./setup.sh --quadlet lays it all down; full runbook in Hardened deployment.

docs.title: Architecture review — August 2026
docs.text:
Deepening opportunities found by walking the hot spots of the preceding ~50 commits. Vocabulary is deliberate: module (interface + implementation), interface (everything a caller must know, not just the signature), depth (behaviour per unit of interface), seam (where an interface lives), adapter (a thing satisfying an interface at a seam), leverage (what callers gain), locality (what maintainers gain).

Two rules of thumb applied throughout: the deletion test — if deleting a module concentrates complexity it earns its keep, if it merely moves it the module was a pass-through — and one adapter is a hypothetical seam, two is a real one.

Candidate 01 (the duplicated Federation Membership card) shipped as #361. The four below are open, in the order I would take them.

docs.title: 02 — "What a Member may see of a Session" has no home
docs.text:
Strength: strong.

Files: backend/app/sessions/router.py (~280–350), app/sessions/ical.py, app/sessions/models.py.

Problem. Three read paths each re-derive the same rule in their own handler body:

  • GET /sessions composes _strip_coach_notes(_strip_cancelled(...));
  • GET /sessions/{id} writes result["coach_notes"] = None inline and does not filter cancelled sessions;
  • ical.py carries a third, prose-documented allow-list.

_normalize_instance must additionally be remembered at five call sites. This is an authorisation rule scattered across handlers: it is reachable only through an ASGI request, so every test of it costs an authenticated client, and a fourth read endpoint is correct only if its author copies carefully.

Proposed shape. app/sessions/projection.py, owning one question — what does a caller with this Role see?

visible_session(record, *, role)
visible_sessions(records, *, role)

Behind that interface: normalisation to SessionInstanceRead, cancellation filtering, and admin-only field redaction. Handlers keep what is genuinely HTTP. This is the shape app/sessions/templates.py established for the Session Template lifecycle in #352, applied to reads instead of writes.

Payoff. The next admin-only field on a Session is redacted once. Redaction becomes a table test with no request, no DB, no fixtures — alongside test_checkin_window.py, which already has that shape.

docs.title: 03 — The repository seam speaks dict[str, Any]
docs.text:
Strength: worth exploring. Right direction, wrong as a big bang.

Scale: 240 occurrences across 26 modules under backend/app/; backend/tests/fake_repositories.py is 673 lines.

Problem. Every repository Protocol returns an untyped dict, so the interface is not the signature — it is every key name, every "this is an ISO string, not a date" convention, and every default, none of which a type checker can hold. The cost is visible: callers write date.fromisoformat(template["start_date"]), routers re-apply _normalize_* to fill missing optionals, and the fake repositories re-implement the dict shaping the real ones do, because the shape is written down nowhere else.

History confirms it hurts. #345 "settle the date type at the repository seam"; #345 "delete the date guards the member stubs were propping up"; #348 "one member fake for eleven partial stubs".

Proposed shape. Repositories return the Pydantic Read models models.py already defines. The seam does not move; only its currency changes. SessionInstanceRead becomes the return type, _normalize_instance disappears, and the fake constructs the same model as the real repository. app/member_federations/ already has a typed MemberFederationRecord — the precedent exists.

Sequencing. One repository per PR under the existing red-green slicing, starting with sessions. Judge after the first before spreading.

docs.title: 04 — The load / save / error ladder, repeated
docs.text:
Strength: worth exploring.

Files: AdminSettingsPage.tsx (47 useState, 1405 lines), MemberDetailPage.tsx (36), SessionDetailPage.tsx (27), SettingsPage.tsx (20).

Problem. Every card re-declares the same ladder — data, loading, loadError, saveStatus, saveError — plus a useEffect(fetch).then(set).catch(setError) and a try/catch save handler. Each is a shallow module: the interface (the state names) is as large as the implementation (two setters and a fetch), and nothing is shared, so changing how API failures surface is a thirty-site edit.

Proposed shape. Two hooks in frontend/src/lib/, built on the request/isApiError module api/client.ts already centralises (#343):

useResource(fetcher, deps)  -> { data, error, reload }
useAction(fn)               -> { run, status, error }

Deliberately stops short of TanStack Query, which brings caching and invalidation nobody has asked for.

Payoff. Cards shed ~10 lines of state plumbing each and become nearly pure render functions, which the existing __tests__/ suite is good at.

docs.title: 05 — The current User is fetched once per page
docs.text:
Strength: speculative. Listed for completeness; do not start here.

Files: App.tsx plus six pages calling getMe(); 45 isAdmin references; contexts/DojoSettingsProvider.tsx and contexts/ThemeProvider.tsx as the established pattern.

Problem. The Role of the current User is global knowledge being re-derived locally, then threaded down as a prop.

Why it stays speculative. The duplicate fetches are cheap, the threading is harmless, and isAdmin as an explicit prop makes components easier to render in tests than a context would. Revisit if a third Role appears and the boolean stops being enough.

docs.title: Incidental findings
docs.text:
• GET /sessions/{id} does not filter cancelled sessions for a non-admin, while GET /sessions does. Folded into candidate 02, but it is a live inconsistency today.
  • UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md gained Federation Membership with #361. No CONTEXT.md or docs/adr/ exists in this repo, so no candidate here contradicts a recorded decision — there are none to contradict.

docs.title: Calibrating AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS
docs.text: Issue #268. Supersedes the unmeasured 50ms default introduced with the constant-time floor in #255.

docs.title: What the setting does
docs.text:
The passkey "begin" endpoints answer for any email, registered or not, so that a caller cannot tell the two apart from the response. The real path (known email, valid invite) does strictly more work than the decoy path — an extra SELECT, a pending_challenge UPDATE, a commit — and #255 measured that asymmetry at a ~2ms median delta: enough to enumerate registered emails from latency alone.

ConstantTimeAuthMiddleware closes it by holding every request to these paths for a fixed minimum wall-clock time:

  • POST /auth/register/passkey/begin
  • POST /auth/login/passkey/begin
  • POST /auth/invites/redeem/begin

The masking only works while the real path finishes under the floor. Once a real request overruns it there is nothing left to pad, and the delta is observable again. So the floor has to sit above the real path's p99 — which is what this document measures, because 50ms was picked as a round number and never checked against PostgreSQL.

docs.title: How to reproduce the measurement
docs.text:
The harness is backend/tests/test_auth_begin_calibration.py. It is skipped unless AUTH_BEGIN_BENCH=1, so it costs the normal suite nothing.

docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm \
  -e PYTEST_TARGET=tests/test_auth_begin_calibration.py \
  -e AUTH_BEGIN_BENCH=1 \
  -e AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS=1 \
  -e RATE_LIMIT_PER_IP=1000000/minute \
  -e PYTEST_ADDOPTS=-s \
  test > /tmp/bench.log 2>&1

The floor is dropped to 1ms so the measurement captures the endpoint's own work rather than the pad, and the per-IP rate limit is lifted because every sample arrives from one address. Those two overrides belong only to this command. Together they disable the timing-side-channel defence and the brute-force rate limit; never copy them into a deployed environment file. The harness itself cannot run anywhere dangerous — conftest.py refuses any DATABASE_URL that is not a PostgreSQL database with "test" in its name — but the env vars would apply anywhere. It seeds real accounts, members and invites; drives 1000 measured requests per scenario over real HTTP against the uvicorn that run_tests.sh starts; and then asserts the side effects only the real path produces, so a seeding mistake cannot quietly report decoy-path timings as good news.

Two views come out of one run. The harness prints client-observed latency. The numbers below are the server-side elapsed that ConstantTimeAuthMiddleware logs — with the floor at 1ms its "floor exceeded" warning fires on every request and carries the elapsed time. That is the quantity the floor is actually compared against, so it is the one the default has to clear. Extract it with:

grep -a "floor exceeded" /tmp/bench.log

docs.title: Measured results
docs.text: Environment: docker-compose.test.yml (PostgreSQL 16, default fsync=on), podman on WSL2, developer workstation, 2026-08-10. n=1000 per row after 50 discarded warmup requests. All figures in milliseconds, server-side.

docs.title: Sequential — one request at a time
docs.text:
endpoint p50 p90 p95 p99 max login/passkey/begin 7.4 9.0 9.6 11.0 14.2 register/passkey/begin 12.1 14.3 15.1 16.7 27.9 invites/redeem/begin 12.4 14.4 15.1 16.8 23.8

Real-path p99 is 16.8ms; the worst single request out of 3000 was 27.9ms.

docs.title: Under concurrency
docs.text:
Swept on register/passkey/begin, the heaviest repeatable path. "over 50ms" is the share of requests that would have breached the old default.

in-flight requests p50 p90 p99 max over 50ms 1 12.1 14.3 16.7 27.9 0% 2 15.1 18.0 22.1 30.0 0% 4 33.1 38.6 45.7 53.2 0.3% 8 67.1 89.3 167.0 183.0 98.5% 12 108.0 153.5 281.1 339.2 100% 20 206.6 356.7 534.7 553.6 100%

Latency is dominated by queueing, not by the database: past ~4 simultaneous requests the single uvicorn worker's event loop is the bottleneck and every figure scales with concurrency.

docs.title: Re-measured for #432 — one email, on the Member
docs.text:
#432 changed every query on these paths: users.email is gone, and an Account is found by joining its Member on members.email. Registration and invite redemption now create the Account from a Member id (invite redemption creates that Member first when there is none). Same command, same environment class, 2026-10-03:

endpoint p50 p90 p95 p99 max login/passkey/begin 5.0 5.7 5.9 6.5 32.9 register/passkey/begin 5.3 6.0 6.3 6.8 11.0 invites/redeem/begin 7.8 9.0 9.4 10.5 20.7

Server-side, sequential, n=1000 per row after 50 warmups. The join costs nothing measurable: every p99 is below the August figures, which says more about the workstation on the day than about the change. The worst single request, 32.9ms, is a third of the 100ms floor, so the default stands. The concurrency sweep kept its shape: queueing past ~4 requests in flight, as above.

Parity between known and unknown emails is a separate check, and it is still the one that gates: test_passkey_timing.py and test_timing_convergence.py assert that the real and decoy paths converge, and both pass against the new queries.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The default is raised from 50ms to 100ms.

  • At the concurrency a single-dojo instance actually sees, the real path's p99 is 16.8ms and its observed worst case 27.9ms. 50ms did clear both — the old default was not wrong, just unevidenced.
  • It did not clear them by much. These numbers come from a developer workstation; the real path's cost is dominated by the commit, and a production volume on modest VPS storage can be several times slower than an overlay filesystem on a laptop. A 2× slower commit puts the observed maximum at ~56ms, past the old floor. 100ms absorbs that; 50ms does not.
  • The pad itself is cheap. The unit-of-work commits and releases its connection inside the measured region, so a padded request holds an idle asyncio task and no database connection. At the 20/min per-IP limit, doubling the hold time changes in-flight occupancy by a fraction of a request per source — the DoS analysis in #266 is unaffected.
  • 100ms is still well below the threshold at which a user notices latency on a deliberate action like starting a login.

No floor survives a saturated server. At 8 simultaneous begin requests the p99 is already 167ms, and holding that would need a floor an order of magnitude above anything sane. Raising the floor is not the remedy for saturation:

  • The condition is detectable. ConstantTimeAuthMiddleware logs a warning naming the elapsed and configured times on every overrun. Alert on it.
  • The remedy is capacity or rate limiting — a second worker, or a tighter RATE_LIMIT_PER_IP — not a larger AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS. Reaching 4+ simultaneous begin requests requires many distinct source addresses, given the 20/min per-IP limit, which is itself the signal worth acting on.

docs.title: The convergence assertion's own false-failure rate
docs.text: Separately from the floor, backend/tests/timing_support.py asserts that the real and decoy paths converge in latency. Its tolerance is calibrated against the noise in the run being judged, but floored at the 1ms budget inherited from

docs.title: 255 — so on a quiet run, where 3 × control falls under that floor, the
docs.text:
calibration is switched off by its own lower bound and the run is judged against a flat 1ms. Every observed false failure lived in that regime (#364): same-path controls of 0.08–0.20ms against cross-path deltas of 1.12–1.34ms, on three unrelated branches including main.

Raising the floor is not available as a remedy — it is the #255 budget, and it would eat the margin MAX_TOLERANCE_S deliberately leaves under the ~2.02ms leak that issue measured. Instead a tripped assertion is re-measured from scratch and fails only if it reproduces (assert_latency_converges_sampled). A false failure is a per-run sampling accident; a real asymmetry is present on every run.

Measured by Monte Carlo, two branches drawn from an identical distribution at the #298 noise level (±3ms spread, n=31, 100,000 trials):

rounds required false-failure rate 1 5.503% 2 (shipped) 0.317%

Detection is unaffected for every leak shape the suite has a fixture for; the per-shape figures and the one shape that does pay for it are tabulated in the timing_support.py module docstring. Cost is one extra sampling round on the failing path only.

docs.title: Why a confirmed failure is worth reading
docs.text:
#360 asked for the delta to be measured directly, isolated and under load, before any bound was touched — a load-dependent real asymmetry and a sampling accident look alike in a single run. Sampling the redeem-begin pair over 15 rounds per condition, varying only the number of tasks contending for the event loop:

contending tasks signed median delta valid slower control 0 +0.001 ms 8/15 0.173 ms 1 −0.019 ms 7/15 0.149 ms 2 +0.005 ms 8/15 0.136 ms 4 +1.514 ms 15/15 1.139 ms

Unloaded, the delta is nil and its sign is a coin flip — the fingerprint of a sampling accident, and the regime every observed false failure came from. Under real contention the sign stops flipping, and the middleware logs Constant-time floor exceeded ... 169.3ms elapsed vs 20ms floor alongside it. That is not the harness misreading noise: the real path's work has overrun AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS, the floor has stopped masking it, and while the load lasts the asymmetry is as visible to an attacker as to the test.

docs.title: 360 poses the choice as inherent to the endpoint, fix at source versus
docs.text:
load-induced, make the calibration load-robust. The measurement says neither. The observed false failures had quiet controls (0.08–0.20 ms), and the quiet rows above show no delta to be robust to — under 0.02 ms, sign random. They are accidents in the tail of that distribution. The loaded row is a different event, and a true positive: the floor really has stopped masking, so damping it with a quiet phase or a load term would suppress the one reading worth having. What remains is to tell accident from asymmetry by whether it recurs.

Confirmation therefore suppresses the accident without suppressing the unmasking — the accident gets a fresh coin and mostly does not recur, the unmasking holds for as long as the machine is busy. So 0.317% is the floor of the achievable rate rather than a promise, and a failure that survives both rounds should be read as check whether the floor was exceeded — which is what the assertion message now says.

docs.title: CI reports these assertions; it does not gate on them
docs.text:
Since the confirmation round shipped, this assertion has failed 2 of 6 runs on GitHub's hosted runners — against the 0.317% predicted above. Both failures reproduced across both rounds, so whatever drives them persists rather than resampling away, and the independence the 0.317% assumes does not hold there.

Neither documented mechanism explains it. The most recent failure had:

  • same-path control 0.026 ms — an exceptionally quiet run, not a contended one
  • cross-path delta 1.317 ms
  • no Constant-time floor exceeded warning anywhere in the run, so every request finished inside the floor and both paths should have been padded to the same total

Two hypotheses were tested and ruled out:

Hypothesis Test Result Response length differs between paths Compared bodies directly Byte-identical, 1045 both — #354's equalisation holds Residual is the post-response UoW teardown, outside the padded region Raised the floor 20 ms → 200 ms under identical load +3.529 ms → +0.072 ms. A residual outside the padded region could not be absorbed by a larger floor, so it is inside it

So the local contention case is understood (the real path approaches the floor, the mask stops working, a larger floor absorbs it) and the CI case is not.

Given that, .github/workflows/backend-tests.yml marks the three wall-clock assertions timing_sensitive and runs them in a continue-on-error step. The numbers stay visible for anyone investigating, while unrelated PRs stop being painted red — a check that cries wolf trains people to re-run without reading, which is how a real regression gets waved through. The strict assertion is kept where a human is already reading output: a local run, and the full suite on release-candidate tags (tests.yml), which does not exclude them.

A green push is therefore not evidence these converged. If the advisory step fails on a run whose control is not unusually quiet, investigate rather than dismiss.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Measured on a developer workstation, not on UAT or production hardware. The 100ms figure carries deliberate headroom for that reason, but it is not a substitute for the real thing. The cheapest confirmation is the one #268 suggests: check UAT/production logs for "Constant-time floor exceeded". If it never fires under real use, the floor is comfortable. If it fires regularly on an unsaturated instance, the real path there is slower than measured here and this document should be re-run and revised.
  • The measurement uses one uvicorn worker, matching the deployed container. Adding workers would move the concurrency knee but not the sequential figures.
  • These are server-side times. A client also pays network latency, which does not help an attacker — it is added to both the real and the decoy path.

docs.title: Hardened deployment
docs.text:
What an operator graduates to from the Quick self-host: a hardened, self-hosted deployment on rootless Podman + Quadlet, fronted by Traefik for automatic HTTPS. Primary target: AlmaLinux 10 (Podman 5.x). A Debian/Ubuntu stub is at the end.

Architecture at a glance. The app image serves both the built SPA and the /api from one FastAPI container on port 8000. Three containers run per host:

           :80/:443 (host)
               │
         ┌─────▼─────┐        kendo-edge (external)
         │  traefik  │◄───────────────┐
         └───────────┘                │
                                 ┌─────▼─────┐   kendo-backend (isolated)
                                 │    app    │◄──────────────┐
                                 └───────────┘               │
                                                       ┌──────▼─────┐
                                                       │  postgres  │
                                                       └────────────┘
  • kendo-edge — Traefik ↔ app. Traefik is the only container publishing host ports.
  • kendo-backend — app ↔ db, no host ports. The db lives only here, so nothing outside this network can reach it.
  • Both networks set Options=isolate=true, which blocks traffic to containers on other Podman networks while leaving internet egress intact (Traefik still reaches Let's Encrypt).
  • The app straddles both networks; the db is reachable only from the app.

All artifacts referenced below live in deploy/.

UAT and PROD are separate hosts, one instance each. The Quadlet units, Traefik config, and scripts are identical between them — only the per-host env file values and secrets differ.

docs.title: 1. One-time host preparation (as an admin / sudo user)
1.1 Install Podman
docs.text:
sudo dnf install -y podman   # AlmaLinux 10 ships Podman 5.x
podman --version             # confirm >= 4.4 (Quadlet); 5.x expected

docs.title: 1.2 Allow rootless binding of ports 80/443
docs.text:
Rootless containers can't bind ports <1024 by default. Install the provided sysctl drop-in:

sudo install -m 0644 deploy/sysctl-99-kendo-rootless-ports.conf \
  /etc/sysctl.d/99-kendo-rootless-ports.conf
sudo sysctl --system

Trade-off: any unprivileged process may now bind ports ≥80 — fine on a single-purpose appliance. Hardened alternative (keeps the <1024 restriction): leave the sysctl out, set Traefik to publish 8080:80/8443:443, and add a firewalld redirect: 

sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-forward-port=port=443:proto=tcp:toport=8443
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-forward-port=port=80:proto=tcp:toport=8080
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

docs.title: 1.3 Open the firewall
docs.text:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

docs.title: 1.4 Create the dedicated rootless user kendo
docs.text:
A no-login system account owns and runs every container. It is never in sudo/wheel and is never logged into directly.

sudo useradd --create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin kendo
# Verify subuid/subgid ranges exist (auto on AlmaLinux 10); add if missing:
grep -q '^kendo:' /etc/subuid || echo "kendo:200000:65536" | sudo tee -a /etc/subuid
grep -q '^kendo:' /etc/subgid || echo "kendo:200000:65536" | sudo tee -a /etc/subgid

# Linger: start the kendo user manager at boot, keep services running with
# nobody logged in.
sudo loginctl enable-linger kendo

docs.title: 1.5 Get an admin shell as kendo
docs.text:
Always use machinectl — it sets up a proper session bus and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, so systemctl --user works. (su - kendo does not and will leave systemctl --user broken.)

sudo machinectl shell kendo@
# You are now kendo, with a working user systemd session.

Everything from here (sections 2–6) runs as kendo via machinectl shell.

docs.title: 2-4. Lay it all down (as kendo)
docs.text:
# Extract the deployment bundle from the release image — no clone, no build.
# The bundle ships inside the image it configures, so the units below and the
# app they start are one artefact (ADR-0004).
mkdir -p ~/src && cd ~/src
podman run --rm ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:1 init | tar -x

./setup.sh --quadlet

setup.sh --quadlet asks for the domain, the TLS option and the ACME challenge, then does every mechanical step that used to be three sections of transcription here:

  • the five secrets — kendo_postgres_password, kendo_jwt_secret, kendo_database_url, kendo_setup_token, and the DNS-provider token when DNS-01 is chosen. kendo_database_url has to embed the same password as kendo_postgres_password; one script generating both cannot mismatch them. A re-run keeps every existing secret rather than rotating it.
  • the ~/kendo/ tree — kendo-app.env with your domain in all three passkey-bound settings, traefik/traefik.yml with your ACME email and the challenge you picked, traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml with your Host() rule. Plus ~/backups and the backup/restore scripts in ~/.local/bin.
  • the Quadlet units — copied into ~/.config/containers/systemd/, pinned to the tag the bundle was extracted from, then systemctl --user daemon-reload.

It never escalates: the host prerequisites from section 1 are detected and the exact sudo command printed for you to run.

./setup.sh check --quadlet is the preflight, and is safe to run at any time — after an upgrade, after a domain change, or pasted into a bug report. It checks what the app cannot see from inside its container: placeholders left in ~/kendo/, the Host() rule against WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, the certificate the TLS option needs, the podman secrets, DNS for the domain, whether 80/443 are already taken, and the section 1 prerequisites. Every FAIL names its fix and makes it exit non-zero; a warn (DNS resolving to a router's public address behind NAT, say) is informational. It changes nothing and gates nothing — the app still guards its own configuration at startup.

The setup token is printed once. A podman secret cannot be read back, so the value that claims the first admin account (ADR-0003) is shown at the end of the run and nowhere else. Lost means rotate (below), not recover.

Then check, and start the stack:

./setup.sh check --quadlet                     # green? then:
systemctl --user start kendo-traefik.service   # Requires= pulls in app -> migrate -> db
systemctl --user status kendo-db kendo-migrate kendo-app kendo-traefik --no-pager
podman ps
By hand, without setup.sh 
# Config tree the Quadlet units expect at ~/kendo/
mkdir -p ~/kendo/traefik/dynamic ~/backups ~/.local/bin
cp deploy/traefik/traefik.yml            ~/kendo/traefik/traefik.yml
cp deploy/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml      ~/kendo/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml
cp deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example      ~/kendo/kendo-app.env
cp deploy/bin/kendo-backup.sh            ~/.local/bin/ && chmod +x ~/.local/bin/kendo-backup.sh
cp deploy/bin/kendo-restore.sh           ~/.local/bin/ && chmod +x ~/.local/bin/kendo-restore.sh
Then edit the placeholders: - `~/kendo/kendo-app.env` — set `WEBAUTHN_RP_ID`, `WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN`, `CORS_ORIGINS` to your real domain. Leave `TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true` (required behind Traefik — see §6). - `~/kendo/traefik/traefik.yml` — set the ACME `email`, and swap the challenge if HTTP-01 does not suit (§5). - `~/kendo/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml` — set the `Host(...)` rule to your domain. The secrets. These never touch a plaintext env file. Generate strong values and pipe them in (avoid leaving them in shell history — note the leading space or use `read`): 
# 1. Postgres password
printf '%s' 'REPLACE-with-strong-db-password' | podman secret create kendo_postgres_password -

# 2. JWT secret
python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))" | tr -d '\n' \
  | podman secret create kendo_jwt_secret -

# 3. Full DATABASE_URL (must embed the SAME password as #1)
printf '%s' 'postgresql+asyncpg://kendo:REPLACE-with-strong-db-password@kendo-db:5432/kendo' \
  | podman secret create kendo_database_url -

# 4. Setup token — gates claiming the first admin account (ADR-0003). Create it
#    BEFORE first boot: the app refuses to start without it, and whoever holds
#    it is who can claim admin.
openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n' \
  | podman secret create kendo_setup_token -
A fifth, `kendo_dns_token`, only when you use DNS-01 — with the drop-in from §5. Then the units: 
mkdir -p ~/.config/containers/systemd
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.network   ~/.config/containers/systemd/
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.volume    ~/.config/containers/systemd/
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.container ~/.config/containers/systemd/

# Quadlet generates systemd units from these files on daemon-reload.
systemctl --user daemon-reload

The DB host in DATABASE_URL is kendo-db — the container name, resolved by Podman's DNS on the kendo-backend network.

This is why that network uses Options=isolate=true rather than Internal=true (#281): Podman disables DNS on internal networks, so kendo-db would not resolve and kendo-app could never connect. isolate=true keeps DNS while still blocking cross-network traffic by IP. The trade is that the database keeps an outbound route; on Podman that cannot be removed without also losing name resolution.

To rotate a secret later: podman secret rm <name> then recreate, and systemctl --user restart the affected unit.

Because the user has linger enabled and the units declare WantedBy=default.target, the stack now starts automatically on boot. No enable step is needed for .container units generated by Quadlet — the [Install] section handles it after daemon-reload.

Watch the first cert issuance:

podman logs -f kendo-traefik   # look for successful ACME / certificate obtained

Migrations run as their own unit: kendo-migrate.service runs alembic upgrade head and exits, and kendo-app is ordered after it, so the app never serves against a half-migrated schema and a failed migration shows up as a failed kendo-migrate.service rather than as an app crash (#391). systemctl --user status kendo-migrate --no-pager shows the last run.

docs.title: 5. TLS options
docs.text:
setup.sh --quadlet asks this question and writes the answer; this section is what it writes, for a deployment configured by hand or changed later.

  • HTTP-01 (default). Needs inbound port 80. Nothing beyond the httpChallenge block already in traefik.yml.
  • TLS-ALPN-01. Inbound 443 only — the answer when an ISP blocks 80. Replace the httpChallenge block with tlsChallenge: {}.
  • DNS-01. No inbound ports at all (e.g. UAT on a local network). Replace the httpChallenge block with a dnsChallenge naming your lego provider, and give Traefik the credentials as a drop-in — the unit itself stays provider-neutral, and a drop-in survives re-copying the unit on upgrade:
printf '%s' 'REPLACE-with-provider-token' | podman secret create kendo_dns_token -
d=~/.config/containers/systemd/kendo-traefik.container.d && mkdir -p "$d"
printf '[Container]\nEnvironment=CF_DNS_API_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/dns_token\nSecret=kendo_dns_token,type=mount,target=dns_token\n' > "$d/10-dns-01.conf"
systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user restart kendo-traefik

CF_DNS_API_TOKEN is Cloudflare's variable (scope the token to Zone:DNS:Edit on one zone); use whichever your provider documents. A provider that needs several variables needs one Environment=/Secret= pair each. - Bring-your-own cert (internal CA / purchased wildcard). For hosts that can't use Let's Encrypt. See deploy/traefik/dynamic/byo-cert.yml.example — it documents the certs/ bind mount (with the required :Z SELinux label) and the router change. setup.sh --quadlet writes both, the mount as a 20-byo-cert.conf drop-in; the cert and key are yours to drop in ~/kendo/traefik/certs/.

docs.title: 6. Why TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true is required behind Traefik
docs.text:
With Traefik in front, every request's peer IP is Traefik's container IP. The app's rate limiting is keyed on client IP — left unadjusted every visitor shares one bucket, so a single busy client exhausts the limit for everyone. Setting TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true makes the app read the real client IP from X-Forwarded-For.

This is the only rate limiting in the deployment: Traefik's dynamic config carries a security-headers middleware and no RateLimit.

This is safe only because of the network design: the app publishes no host ports and is reachable solely through Traefik, which overwrites any client-supplied X-Forwarded-For (do not enable forwardedHeaders.insecure on Traefik's entrypoints). The flag defaults to false so local dev — where the app is directly reachable — stays spoof-proof.

docs.title: 7. A note on CORS
docs.text: The SPA is served same-origin with the API (both under https://<your-domain>), so CORS never fires in normal operation. Keep CORS_ORIGINS pinned to the single canonical origin (never *) — auth is cookie-based, and * + credentials is both invalid and a credential-leak risk. Pinning means any accidental cross-origin path fails closed.

docs.title: Appendix — Debian / Ubuntu stub (not the primary target)
docs.text:
The above is written for AlmaLinux 10. On Debian/Ubuntu the shape is identical; the differences:

  • Podman version. Debian 12 ships Podman 4.3 — too old for Quadlet. Install ≥4.4 from the Kubic/OCI repo or use Ubuntu 24.04 (Podman 4.9). Ubuntu 24.10+/newer is smoother.
  • No SELinux (AppArmor instead) — the :Z volume labels are harmless no-ops; leave them.
  • Low ports / firewall. net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start works the same via /etc/sysctl.d/. Use ufw instead of firewalld for the redirect alternative.
  • User/linger/machinectl — useradd, loginctl enable-linger, and machinectl shell all work identically (systemd-based).
