docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Authentication has no password column. Passkeys are the only login path (#155); users carries the WebAuthn challenge fields and nothing else. recovery_codes and admin_recovery_tokens hold bcrypt hashes; invites.token_hash is a deterministic sha256 digest (it is looked up by value — see app/auth/invite_service.py for why that differs).
  • recovery_attempts retention (#434). A successful attempt deletes that Account's earlier rows, leaving only the success. Rows that remain (an Account that keeps failing) are kept — lockout counts failures since the last success with no time window, so deleting by age would expire lockouts — but ip_address is cleared to NULL once a row is 30 days old (IP_RETENTION in app/auth/attempt_repository.py). There is no scheduler: the clear runs on every log_attempt, for all Accounts, so an address can outlive 30 days until the next recovery attempt anywhere on the instance.
  • Every Account belongs to exactly one Member (#432, ADR-0006). users.member_id is a live link and is enforced: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and a foreign key to members.id with ON DELETE RESTRICT (Members are deactivated or anonymised, never hard-deleted). Most Members have no Account. The email lives once, on the Member — members.email is both the contact address and the sign-in identifier; users has no email column.
  • Audit columns are not foreign keys. attendance.recorded_by, grade_history.assigned_by and members.anonymised_by record which Account acted. They are deliberately not FK-enforced, so the id outlives the Account it names: erasing a member deletes their Account, and the history that Account recorded must not cascade with it.
  • Constraints beyond keys (#431). The database, not just the app, refuses:
  • uq_attendance_session_member — UNIQUE (session_id, member_id) on attendance: a member is checked in at most once per session. NULLs are distinct, so any number of visitor rows (member_id NULL) per session stay legal. This, not the router's existence check, decides a concurrent double check-in (the loser gets 409).
  • ck_attendance_member_xor_visitor — CHECK on attendance: exactly one of member_id / visitor_name is set.
  • uq_member_federations_member_federation — UNIQUE (member_id, federation_id): one membership per member per federation.
  • uq_dojo_settings_single_row — a unique index on the constant (true): dojo_settings holds one row.
  • uq_federations_name — UNIQUE federations.name.
  • Federation membership is a table, not a column. members has no federation_number: a member can hold numbers with several federations, so it lives in member_federations (dropped from members in #297 — see a5b6c7d8e9f0_drop_federation_number_from_members.py).
  • Sessions are segmented. session_templates/session_instances carry no single session_type_id/start_time/duration_minutes. Each session has one or more segments, each with its own start_time/duration_minutes/ optional public title/position, and each segment links to one or more session types via the *_segment_types join tables (also ordered by position). A session's time envelope (for calendar display) is derived as min(segment start) → max(segment end) — see app/sessions/envelope.py. Segments have no notes of their own: per-segment coach_notes went in #190 and the public per-segment note in #406. Prose about a session belongs in the session-level info (public) or coach_notes (admin-only).
  • session_instances.title is required (no longer derived from session type).
  • session_instances.checkin_window_* override the dojo-wide defaults in dojo_settings when set; null means "use the dojo default".
  • All *_segments/*_segment_types child rows cascade-delete with their parent (ondelete="CASCADE" at the DB level, cascade="all, delete-orphan" at the ORM level) and are fully replaced (delete+recreate) on update — there is no row-level PATCH of an individual segment.

docs.title: The app serves the SPA and the API from one origin, with the API under /api
docs.text: The built SPA is copied into the app image and served by FastAPI itself, and every API router is mounted under an /api prefix, so browser and API share a single origin in development, the quick self-host and the hardened deployment alike. /health (used by container healthchecks) and the /static/* upload mounts stay at the root.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The frontend already called /api/..., but the routers were mounted at the root and Vite's dev proxy rewrote the prefix away. That worked only in development: in both production stacks / and /api/* returned 404, because nothing served the SPA and no route answered the prefixed paths — despite docs/deployment.md describing exactly this arrangement. Single-origin also keeps cookie-based auth and WebAuthn simple: no CORS preflight on the app's own calls, no cross-site cookie rules, one origin for WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN to match.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: Letting the reverse proxy own the split instead — Traefik routing /api to the backend with a StripPrefix middleware and / to a separate SPA container — was rejected. It contradicts the hardened deployment's single kendo-app container, adds a container and a middleware to production for no gain, and leaves the app image unable to serve itself when run without a proxy.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The SPA catch-all mount is conditional on static/index.html existing, so the development image (which runs from source, with Vite serving the frontend) does not need a build step. Vite's /api rewrite is gone: development and production now use identical URLs, which is what makes a proxy in front of the dev stack meaningful at all — see ADR-0002.

docs.title: Traefik runs in the development stack
docs.text: The development Compose stack runs Traefik in front of the app, serving https://dojo.localhost:8443 with a locally-generated certificate, and .env.dev sets COOKIE_SECURE=true and TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true to match the hardened deployment.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A reverse proxy in a dev stack looks like gratuitous machinery. It is there for three behaviours that are otherwise exercised for the first time in production: passkey ceremonies bound to a real WEBAUTHN_RP_ID/WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN over TLS, Secure session cookies, and the X-Forwarded-For path that rate limiting and account lockout depend on. Each of these fails silently or not at all in a plain-HTTP localhost:5173 stack, and each produces a healthy-looking deployment that rejects logins or mis-attributes client IPs.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: dojo.localhost needs no /etc/hosts entry (browsers resolve *.localhost to loopback) and is a secure context, so it beats a .test domain. Ports 8443/8080 are used rather than 443/80 so that running the dev stack does not require the net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start sysctl; the port appears in WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN but not in WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, which stays the bare host. Traefik is configured through the file provider, as in deploy/quadlet — the socket-based label provider was rejected there deliberately and copying it into development would diverge exactly where the point is to match.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The dev certificate is now on the critical path for any authenticated work: with COOKIE_SECURE=true and browsers refusing WebAuthn on a page with a certificate error, an untrusted certificate presents as a healthy stack that cannot hold a session — so make certs reports what it issued and reissues a self-signed pair once mkcert appears, and the README carries the trust-store split a container cannot resolve on the developer's behalf (#379).

The direct :5173 and :8000 ports stay published as an escape hatch when a certificate is missing or HMR misbehaves through the proxy, so the proxy is never the only way in. Vite needs explicit HMR client settings to serve through it, derived from DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN so that the no-proxy runs (the test container, a bare npm run dev) keep dialling their own origin. Host and scheme come from that origin; the client port is pinned only when the origin names one, so a portless origin behind a proxy on 443 leaves Vite to infer the port from the page and keeps its direct-websocket fallback (#380). server.ws is server-wide and Vite's direct-websocket fallback is skipped once a client port is pinned, so exactly one of the two published origins can have HMR: DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN is interpolated with the proxy origin as its default, and emptying it hands HMR to the :5173 escape hatch — which matters when the reason for taking that hatch is HMR misbehaving through the proxy (#382). allowedHosts turned out to be unnecessary: Vite allows localhost and any *.localhost host header before it consults that list. The test stack deliberately does not get Traefik: the e2e suite drives Vite and uvicorn in one container, and an ~11 minute suite should not grow a proxy hop for fidelity it does not test.

docs.title: Claiming the first admin account requires a pre-provisioned setup token
docs.text: The operator provisions a SETUP_TOKEN before first boot — a podman secret injected as env under Quadlet, a value in the env file for the Compose self-host — and POST /api/setup/passkey/complete requires it. The app reads it from config like any other secret, compares it in constant time, and refuses to start without it. /api/setup/passkey/begin requires it too (see the amendment under Consequences); GET /api/setup is unchanged, and the existing _has_registered_user() guard still runs first, so a claimed instance stays 404 regardless of what token is presented.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
/api/setup, /api/setup/passkey/begin and /api/setup/passkey/complete are unauthenticated and guarded only by _has_registered_user() — count( PasskeyCredential) > 0 — and complete promotes whoever finishes the ceremony to role="admin". Until someone deliberately finishes, anyone who loads the page takes the dojo (#388).

Counting credentials rather than users is correct and stays: an abandoned ceremony leaves a user row with no credential, and counting those would lock out an operator whose browser died mid-registration. The consequence is that the window never closes on its own.

The hostname is not a secret. Traefik's Let's Encrypt certificate reaches the certificate transparency logs the moment it is issued, so a public deployment is discoverable by an opportunistic scanner within minutes of first boot — plausibly before the operator has opened a browser. The only mitigation today is a paragraph in docs/deployment.md telling the operator to claim the account immediately, which asks them to win a race they were not told they were in until they read it.

That opportunistic scanner is the realistic attacker, not someone targeting this dojo by name. The LAN UAT box and the public PROD box therefore differ in exposure but not in the right policy: the LAN box is simply one the attacker rarely reaches, and a policy that only PROD gets is a policy that is wrong on the day a UAT box gets a public DNS name. One policy covers both.

The deployment already has the shape this needs. deploy/quadlet/kendo-app.container injects two podman secrets as environment:

Secret=kendo_database_url,type=env,target=DATABASE_URL
Secret=kendo_jwt_secret,type=env,target=JWT_SECRET

A third entry is a line of unit file and a podman secret create. Nothing in the app has to learn a new way to hold a secret, and nothing has to learn a new way to hand one to the operator.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
A pre-provisioned SETUP_TOKEN (chosen). It is config, not state: no table, no migration, no process-scoped value to re-fetch, and no retrieval path to invent. It survives restarts, which matters under Restart=always — a crash-looping unclaimed instance must not invalidate the token the operator is part-way through using. It does not require shell access from the person who claims the account, so an operator can hand a URL and a token to a dojo secretary. Rotation is podman secret rm/create plus a restart.

Its costs are real and accepted. It adds a step before first boot, which the deployment runbook must carry. The plaintext exists wherever the operator generated it — shell history, unless they pipe it (openssl rand -base64 32 | podman secret create kendo_setup_token -). Under Compose there are no podman secrets, so it lives in the same env file that already holds the database password: the same exposure class as what is there, not a new one.

A token generated at boot and printed to the container log. Attractive because podman logs kendo-app is already in the day-2 table, and it needs no provisioning step. Rejected on the Quadlet specifics. Container stdout goes to journald, so the token persists at journald's retention rather than in something ring-buffer-shaped, and log aggregation would carry it off-box; "the token dies with the process" bounds its validity, not where the string is written. Worse, Restart=always means an unclaimed instance that crash-loops issues a fresh token per restart, silently invalidating the one the operator copied a minute ago and failing their correctly-filled form with a 401. The runbook would have to say "re-read the logs after any restart", which is a bad instruction to have to give during first setup.

A token minted through the CLI (app/cli.py, alongside create-recovery-token), retrieved with podman exec kendo-app .... This works with no extra wiring — DATABASE_URL is already injected as env and exec inherits it — and keeps the secret out of the journal. Rejected because it needs persisted token state, a table and a migration, to deliver a secret that config can carry for free, and because it makes shell access a hard requirement for first setup, which forecloses handing a URL to a non-technical dojo secretary.

A pre-seeded admin email in the env file, with setup refusing any other address, carries no new secret and uses a value the operator already sets per host. Rejected as insufficient alone: it authenticates an address, not a person, so a scanner that guesses or learns the dojo's contact address is back inside the window. It narrows the race rather than closing it.

Binding the window to a boot deadline — setup answers only within N minutes of process start — composes with anything here but does not stop this attacker. A CT-log scanner arrives within minutes of first boot, inside any window generous enough not to strand an operator on a slow start, and the option adds a liveness and clock dependency for that partial benefit. Not adopted; revisit only if the token proves insufficient.

Keeping setup open and making it observable would be the honest minimum if the current design were right for this threat model. It is not: the problem is an unbounded window on a publicly discoverable host, not the absence of a signal about it. The observability is not lost — an unclaimed instance still logs one startup line saying so, carrying the claim URL and no secret.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
A missing SETUP_TOKEN fails startup, claimed or not. It joins _REQUIRED_STARTUP_VARS in app/config.py alongside JWT_SECRET and DATABASE_URL, so a misconfigured deployment dies at boot with a named error instead of booting into a claimable instance. Validating it only while the instance is unclaimed was considered and rejected: it needs a database query in lifespan() to decide, and it invites an operator to delete the secret after claiming — which boots fine until the day the database is restored or wiped, and then fails at exactly the wrong moment. One unconditional rule is smaller and fails in the safe direction. .env.example gains the variable, and development needs a value like any other required secret.

Redeploy against an existing database does not reopen anything. Claimed state lives in PasskeyCredential rows; the existing guard runs first, so a restarted or upgraded claimed instance returns 404 as it does today. The token is a second gate in front of that guard, never a replacement for it — and an instance whose token leaks after it is claimed is not thereby claimable.

No migration and no new state. The token is a config value compared with secrets.compare_digest at complete. It travels as an X-Setup-Token header rather than a body field: the request models are shared with the ordinary registration route, and a header keeps the secret out of them and out of anything that logs a request body. GET /setup stays open so the SPA can decide whether to render the setup page.

Amended during implementation (#402). begin is gated too. This ADR originally left it open on the grounds that it closes nothing complete does not already close. That is true of the claim itself, but not of the side effects: begin on an unclaimed instance runs the bootstrap branch of _get_or_create_user, which writes a user row with role="admin" for any email a stranger submits. Leaving it open lets an unauthenticated scanner accumulate admin-roled credential-less rows. Both endpoints now call one shared _require_setup_token() — one place to get the check wrong, not two — after _has_registered_user(), so 404 still wins on a claimed instance.

The same amendment closes the route the original decision missed entirely. POST /api/auth/register/passkey/begin is unauthenticated and reaches the same bootstrap branch, so gating only /setup/* would have left the claim open to anyone who read the OpenAPI schema. The branch is therefore gated where every caller routes through it — register_passkey_begin and register_passkey_complete take allow_bootstrap, which only the setup router passes, and only after the token check. On an unclaimed instance the ordinary registration route now answers with the same decoy it gives an unknown email on a claimed one.

Lockout is a rotation, not a rebuild. An operator who loses the token recreates the secret and restarts; nothing in the database has to change. The existing break-glass path does not cover a never-claimed instance and is not being stretched to — app/cli.py create-recovery-token resolves a User row by email, and on an unclaimed instance there is none. That gap is acceptable because rotation costs seconds.

The runbook gains a step and loses a race. docs/deployment.md currently tells the operator to claim the account before a stranger does; it will instead tell them to create the secret before first boot. The curl /api/setup check stays useful and its meaning is unchanged.

docs.title: Deployments run a published image pinned by major tag
docs.text: Tagged releases build the prod stage and push to GHCR as ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement with 1.0.0, 1.0, 1 and latest. Both deployment paths reference that image — docker-compose.yml in place of build: ., deploy/quadlet/kendo-app.container and kendo-migrate.container in place of localhost/kendodojo:latest — and the documented pin for an operator is the major tag, :1. The image also carries the deployment bundle it needs — the compose file, the .example config, the Quadlet units, the backup scripts and setup.sh — extracted with podman run --rm <image> init | tar -x, so an operator never clones. Building from source stays supported and becomes optional.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every operator today must clone the repository and run make build before anything starts. That is the single largest barrier to a stranger self-hosting this: it requires a git checkout, a working build toolchain on the target host, and several minutes of build time before the first line of the setup instructions has any visible effect. The target operator for the quick self-host is a technical hobbyist with a VPS and a domain — not someone who wants to own a build.

A published image removes the toolchain and the build. It does not, on its own, remove the clone: the app is only half of what a host needs, and the other half is text — docker-compose.yml, .env.example, the Traefik .example files, deploy/quadlet/, deploy/bin/kendo-*.sh and the setup.sh that writes them. Publishing the image while leaving that config on the git side gives one deployment two distribution channels on two version axes, and a checkout of main against an image pinned :1 is config from the tip driving an app from 1.x.

It also raises a question the build-on-host model never had to answer: what does an operator write in their config, and what does upgrading mean?

Alembic is the real compatibility surface. The migrate service runs alembic upgrade head against the operator's live database, unattended, before app starts. An operator who pulls a new image is consenting to a schema change whether or not they realise it, and the only true rollback for a migration they did not want is a restore from backup. So the tag an operator pins is not a cosmetic preference — it is the promise the project makes about when their database will change shape under them.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
:latest only. Simplest to publish and simplest to document. Rejected because pull && up -d then drags the operator across any migration at all, including a breaking one, with no way to express "I want fixes but not a schema rewrite". The failure mode is silent and lands on the least experienced operators hardest.

Date tags (:2026-09-13). Unambiguous and trivially ordered, but a date carries no compatibility information. :2026-09-13 to :2026-10-01 tells the operator nothing about whether their data survives, so it solves publishing without solving the question publishing raises.

Semver, pinned by major (chosen). :1 means "fixes and features, no migration that requires a restore". Moving to :2 is an explicit edit the operator makes, at a time of their choosing, having read the release notes. The narrower pins (:1.0, :1.0.0) remain available for operators who want them, and :latest remains for anyone who genuinely wants the tip. Versioned documentation follows the same axis: an operator on :1 reads the 1.x docs.

The same question applies to the config, and the answers are not independent of it — whatever carries the config has to track the same axis the image is pinned on.

Clone the release branch (git clone -b release/1.x). Free in git, one line of documentation. Rejected because it keeps the clone in the install for the sake of 170 KB of text, and leaves the two axes merely conventionally aligned: nothing stops a :1 pin against a main checkout.

A release tarball asset per tag. Correct pinning, but a second artefact to publish, sign and document alongside the image.

curl … | bash bootstrap that fetches the rest at a pinned ref. Removes the clone, but adds bootstrap logic the project owns and a pipe-to-shell install.

The image carries the bundle (chosen). Podman is already the prerequisite and podman run needs no compose file, so the image can hand over its own config before anything is configured: a COPY into /bundle in the prod stage and an init branch in entrypoint.sh that tars it to stdout. Install is three commands and no git. Skew is closed by construction rather than by convention — the bundle comes out of the image it configures, so setup.sh writes that exact tag into .env rather than guessing, and there is one version axis instead of two.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Cutting a major version becomes a real commitment rather than a number. Any migration that cannot be rolled back by re-pointing at the previous image must land in a new major, and the release notes for it have to say what an operator must do. That discipline is the point — it is what makes :1 worth pinning — but it is a constraint on the migration chain that did not exist while every deployment built from source.

GHCR images from a private repository are not anonymously pullable and count against the account's package quota. The documented podman-compose pull path therefore cannot be exercised as a stranger experiences it until the repository is public; until then the workflow is proved by pulling with a token.

localhost/kendodojo:latest remains buildable and is still what a contributor runs. Nothing here removes the build — it stops being mandatory.

The image gains a second mode. entrypoint.sh has been deliberately narrow — one exec uvicorn, with migrations kept out of it so a failed migration never looks like an app crash — and init is the first argument it interprets. It stays a tar to stdout and nothing more: it writes no files, needs no mounts, and cannot be reached once the app is running.

The bundle becomes a shipped surface. Anything under /bundle is published to operators at that tag, so the dev-only paths (deploy/certs/, deploy/traefik/dev/) must stay out of it, and a config change now lands in a release rather than the moment it merges. setup.sh upgrade re-extracts the bundle and reports what changed instead of overwriting an operator's filled-in files.

docs.title: Session Templates and Sessions stay separate tables
docs.text:
Session Templates (the recurring rule) and Sessions (one dated event) are stored as two parallel sets of three tables — session_template{,_segments,_segment_types} and session_instance{,_segments,_segment_types} — with near-identical columns. We keep all six rather than collapsing them into three tables with a discriminator column.

The resemblance is shallower than it looks, and the two have already diverged: a Session carries cancelled and the check-in window overrides, a template carries its recurrence rule (recurrence, day_of_week, recurrence_days, interval_weeks, start_date, end_date). One merged table would have to make every one of those columns nullable and trust application code to know which apply to which kind of row. The segment tables would then need a polymorphic parent — a column that points at either a template or a Session — which a foreign key cannot constrain. Six tables that each say exactly what they hold are worth more than three that need a discriminator to be read correctly.

Decided in the schema review, issue #418.

docs.title: Accounts and Members stay separate tables
docs.text:
A Member is the kendoka: name, email, date of birth, grade, emergency contact, safeguarding data. An Account is how a Member signs in: passkeys, recovery codes, Role (the code still calls it User / users). Every Account belongs to exactly one Member — there is no sign-in without a kendoka, the first Admin included, whose Member is created when they claim the instance. Most Members have no Account. The obvious simplification is one people table; we keep two, linked by a NOT NULL, unique users.member_id, for three reasons.

  • They are deleted differently. Erasure hard-deletes the Account and its credentials but anonymises the Member in place, so attendance and grade history keep a row to point at. A single table would need a tombstone row with every auth column nulled: two tables sharing one row.
  • They are read under different trust conditions. Accounts are looked up by the unauthenticated registration and login endpoints, where enumeration and timing parity have had real work (#239, #267, #300). Members hold the personal and under-18 data. Merging them puts that data on the row that pre-auth lookups load.
  • The roster outlives sign-ins. Most Members never sign in, and a Member who leaves loses their Account but keeps their history.

The email address is stored once, on the Member, and is both the contact address and the sign-in identifier: two copies that must always be equal is one copy. Pre-auth code therefore finds an Account by joining its Member on that one indexed column — it matches on members.email and loads only the Account, never the Member row, so the trust boundary above still holds. Only an Admin can change the address; the app sends no mail, so a self-service change could not be verified.

Decided in the schema review, issue #418.

docs.title: The app connects as a least-privilege database user
docs.text:
The official PostgreSQL image makes POSTGRES_USER (kendo) a superuser, and every process used to connect as it — including the internet-facing web app. A compromised app (SQL injection, code execution in its container) could then run shell commands in the database container with COPY … TO PROGRAM, read and write server files, drop the schema, and create users. The app needs none of that: it never changes the schema at runtime. So the web app and app/cli.py connect as a second database user that can only read and write rows, and kendo stays the superuser for migrations, backup and restore. The goal is to contain a compromised app, not to hide data from it: the app user still reads and writes every app table.

  • Two URLs. DATABASE_URL is the app user's login everywhere; a new MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL holds the superuser login and is given only to the migration step, so the superuser password never reaches the app container.
  • The migration step maintains the app user. app/db/bootstrap.py already runs as superuser before every app start. After alembic upgrade head it creates the user named in DATABASE_URL if missing, sets its password from the secret, and re-applies the grants, on every run: existing volumes are covered, drift is repaired, and rotating the password is changing the secret.
  • Grants: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on app tables, USAGE, SELECT on sequences, SELECT only on alembic_version (so a compromised app cannot fake the schema version), set as default privileges for tables kendo creates later. No TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, REFERENCES or CREATE.
  • No sliding back. The app refuses to start when connected as a superuser, and the e2e tests run the server as the app user, so a missing grant fails in CI rather than tempting someone to point DATABASE_URL back at kendo.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• A third user owning the schema, non-superuser, for migrations, leaving the superuser to backup and restore only. Rejected for now: the migration step is short-lived and on the backend network only, while moving ownership off the bootstrap superuser cannot be done with REASSIGN OWNED and means altering every object. The internet-facing app was the risk worth paying for.
  • Creating the app user in a docker-entrypoint-initdb.d script. Rejected: it runs only on an empty volume, so existing volumes miss it and a password change becomes a manual ALTER ROLE.
  • Grants in an Alembic migration. Rejected: the password is a secret and cannot live in the chain, so user creation would be split across two places.

Decided in issue #453.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Podman + podman-compose (Docker Compose may work — see Container runtime)
  • Python 3.13 + a virtual environment (python3 -m venv backend/.venv)
  • Node 22

docs.title: Get the code
docs.text:
Operators do not need a clone — the release image carries its own deployment bundle (Quick self-host). Contributors do:

git clone https://github.com/booji/KendoDojoManagement.git
cd KendoDojoManagement

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Copy the dev env file (safe to commit — contains no real secrets): 

cp .env.dev .env.dev.local   # optional local overrides

.env.dev is already wired into docker-compose.dev.yml. No edits needed to get started.

docs.title: Start the dev stack
docs.text:
make dev

This starts: - proxy — Traefik, on host ports 8443 (HTTPS) and 8080 (redirect to 8443) - backend — FastAPI with hot-reload on file changes, on host port 8000 - frontend — Vite dev server with HMR, on host port 5173 - db — PostgreSQL 16, published on host port 5433

Open https://dojo.localhost:8443. Browsers resolve *.localhost to loopback, so no /etc/hosts entry is needed, and treat it as a secure context. Traefik routes /api, /health and /static to the backend and everything else to Vite, so the browser sits on one origin for both the UI and the API — the same shape production has (see docs/adr/0001-single-origin-api-under-api-prefix.md).

The proxy is not decoration. .env.dev sets COOKIE_SECURE=true, TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true and a real WEBAUTHN_RP_ID/WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN, so Secure cookies, passkey ceremonies and the X-Forwarded-For path that rate limiting and lockout depend on are exercised here rather than for the first time in production — the reasoning is in docs/adr/0002-traefik-in-the-dev-stack.md.

http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:8000 stay published as an escape hatch for when a certificate is missing or HMR misbehaves through the proxy. On those, cookies are not sent (they are Secure) and X-Forwarded-For is whatever the caller claims — so do not test login or rate limiting there.

Vite's websocket setting is server-wide, so exactly one of the two origins gets working HMR — the proxy by default. To hand it to :5173 instead, start the stack with the proxy origin emptied:

DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN= make dev

Then :5173 live-reloads and https://dojo.localhost:8443 does not (the page still works; changes need a refresh). Put DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN= in .env.dev to make it stick across runs.

docs.title: The dev TLS certificate
docs.text:
The certificate is on the critical path: .env.dev sets COOKIE_SECURE=true, and browsers refuse WebAuthn on a page with a certificate error — so a degraded certificate looks like a perfectly healthy stack right up until the first login or passkey ceremony fails.

1. Generate. make dev runs make certs for you, or run it directly:

make certs         # issue if missing, untrusted, or no longer covering dojo.localhost
make certs-force   # reissue unconditionally (no manual `rm` needed)

It says which generator it used. With mkcert on your PATH the pair is issued by your local CA; without it you get a self-signed pair and a warning saying so. Install mkcert and re-run make certs — it notices the self-signed certificate and reissues. The pair lives in deploy/certs/ and is gitignored: per-machine, never committed.

2. Trust the CA — on the machine the browser runs on. mkcert -install installs the CA into the trust store of the OS it runs on. If the stack and the browser are on different systems, a successful-looking install does nothing for the browser:

Stack runs on Browser runs on Install the CA where Linux (native) the same Linux mkcert -install in that shell WSL2 Windows export $(mkcert -CAROOT)/rootCA.pem from WSL and import it into the Windows store (certutil -addstore -user Root rootCA.pem), or install mkcert on Windows and run mkcert -install there A VM or remote dev box your laptop copy rootCA.pem off the box and import it into the laptop's store

Firefox keeps its own store. It does not read the OS trust store. Either install nss-tools (certutil) before mkcert -install so mkcert can add the CA to Firefox's NSS database, or on Windows set security.enterprise_roots.enabled to true in about:config.

3. Verify. Open https://dojo.localhost:8443 — no warning, and a padlock. That is the whole check; a warning means the browser does not trust the CA, not that the certificate is malformed.

4. Restart the proxy after any reissue. Traefik loads the certificate at startup and its file provider watches the config files, not the certificate bytes. A replaced pair is not picked up until the proxy restarts (make down && make dev), which otherwise looks exactly like the new certificate not working.

When it goes wrong:

Symptom Cause Fix Passkey ceremony fails, everything else looks fine self-signed certificate install mkcert, make certs mkcert -install succeeded but the browser still warns CA is in the wrong OS's trust store see the table above Chrome is happy, Firefox is not Firefox's separate NSS store nss-tools + mkcert -install, or security.enterprise_roots.enabled The old warning persists after reissuing Traefik still serving the startup certificate make down && make dev

If you need to get in without a certificate at all, http://localhost:5173 is still published — but cookies and passkeys do not work there, and HMR only reaches it if the stack was started with DEV_PROXY_ORIGIN= (above).

docs.title: Network layout
docs.text:
Two networks, mirroring the Quadlet production deployment in deploy/quadlet (kendo-edge + kendo-backend):

Network Members Purpose edge proxy, frontend, backend Traefik fronts both; carries the published host ports backend backend, db The only path to PostgreSQL

frontend is not on the backend network. It runs arbitrary npm dependencies with node_modules mounted — the least trusted container in the stack — so it cannot reach the database at all.

Nothing uses network_mode: host any more. Host-networked containers join no Compose network, so there was nothing to segment, and the database ended up binding host port 5432 directly (see below). The browser runs on the host and never joins a Compose network, so browser reachability depends only on published ports: 8443/8080 for the proxy, and the 1:1 5173:5173 and 8000:8000 escape hatches behind it.

Two runtime quirks are worth knowing, both verified on podman 5.6.0:

  • isolate=true is what actually enforces the split. Podman's bridge networks are otherwise mutually routable by IP — the frontend cannot resolve db, but it can open a socket to the database's 10.89.x.x address. The driver_opts in both Compose files close that. Docker isolates user-defined bridges natively, so the option is redundant there — and untested, like everything else on Docker. If a Docker version rejects the driver_opts key, dropping it loses nothing on that runtime.
  • The backend network is not internal: true, unlike Internal=true on kendo-backend.network in deploy/quadlet. Podman disables DNS on internal networks (dnsname and internal networks are incompatible), so the service name db stops resolving and the backend cannot connect. The trade is the database's outbound route, which cannot be removed on Podman without also losing service-name DNS.

docs.title: Why the database is on 5433, not 5432
docs.text:
db publishes a mapped port rather than binding the host's. Host networking used to make it bind host port 5432 directly — the conventional PostgreSQL port. Anything else on the machine holding that port (a system install, another project's stack, a leftover container) claimed it first, and the dev database then exited 1 while podman-compose up -d db still reported success. A published port fails loudly on a collision, and 5433 avoids the common one entirely.

To run two checkouts of this repo side by side, set a different POSTGRES_PORT in .env.dev and change the port in DATABASE_URL in the same file to match. The other four host ports are fixed and will collide: 8443 and 8080 (proxy), 5173 (Vite) and 8000 (uvicorn). Only one checkout's dev stack can be up at a time unless you edit them — and 8443 also appears in WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN, CORS_ORIGINS, the dev routing file and server.hmr.clientPort. The frontend port must stay mapped 1:1 (5173:5173): Vite's HMR client infers the websocket port from the browser's location, so publishing it on a different host port needs server.hmr.clientPort set in frontend/vite.config.ts.

docs.title: Connecting from the host
docs.text:
The port is published on 127.0.0.1 only — the dev credentials are weak and committed to the repo, so the database is deliberately not reachable from the LAN. Host-side tooling (alembic, psql, a one-off script) must point at the published port, not 5432, and address 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost (which can resolve to ::1, where nothing is listening):

export DATABASE_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://kendo_dev:kendo_dev_password@127.0.0.1:5433/kendo_dev
psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5433 -U kendo_dev -d kendo_dev

If you get password authentication failed for user "kendo_dev" on port 5432, you are talking to a different PostgreSQL — the credentials are not the problem, the port is.

docs.title: Make targets
docs.text:
Target What it does make List the targets (starts nothing) make dev Start the hot-reload dev stack make test Start the test watcher (re-runs pytest on every save) make screenshots Regenerate the README / docs sessions screenshots (docs/assets, desktop and mobile, light and dark) from a made-up dojo — rerun after a UI change to the calendar make build Build the production image as localhost/kendodojo:latest (releases run the published image — see ADR-0004) make down Stop the stacks this checkout starts — dev and test make down-selfhost Stop the quick self-host stack — takes the dojo offline make certs Issue the dojo.localhost dev TLS certificate if it is missing or untrusted (run for you by make dev) make certs-force Reissue the dev TLS certificate unconditionally make logs Tail dev service logs make migrate Run alembic upgrade head in the running dev container make help List all targets

The Makefile auto-detects podman-compose vs docker compose, so the targets run under either. That detection is kept because it costs nothing, not because Docker is tested — see Container runtime.

make down deliberately leaves the quick self-host alone: on a machine that is actually serving a dojo, stopping it must be a deliberate act, so it has its own target. The same reasoning already governs make clean refusing to remove the production database volume.

make dev generates a per-machine dojo.localhost certificate under deploy/certs/ (gitignored) if one is missing, self-signed while mkcert is available, or no longer covering the dev host. The full step — generate, trust, verify, reissue, and the failure modes — is The dev TLS certificate.

docs.title: TDD workflow
docs.text: The working agreements live in CLAUDE.md, which people and coding agents follow alike. These are its design and testing sections, included here as written.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Deep modules (Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design): favor small interfaces hiding large implementations. A caller should need to know as little as possible about what's underneath. New modules and abstractions should earn their existence by hiding meaningful complexity.

Abstraction is encouraged where it genuinely aids human readability; avoid speculative abstractions for hypothetical future needs.

docs.title: TDD Workflow
docs.text:
Follow red-green as vertical slices, not horizontal slicing: 1. Write one failing test for the next small behavior. 2. Write the minimum implementation to make it pass. 3. Refactor if needed, then move to the next test.

Never write a full test suite first and then implement everything — that is horizontal slicing and is explicitly not the workflow here.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
make test

This mounts ./backend into a container alongside an ephemeral PostgreSQL instance and re-runs the full suite on every file change. The database is destroyed on make down.

One-shot run inside the running container: 

podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml exec test pytest -q

A one-shot run of the whole suite, with optional pytest flags: 

podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm test
podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm -e PYTEST_ARGS=-x test
podman-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm \
  -e PYTEST_TARGET=tests/test_members.py test

Pass pytest flags through PYTEST_ARGS, not positionally after the service name: podman-compose treats trailing arguments as the container command, so run --rm test -x fails with crun: executable file `-x` not found in $PATH. Only real docker compose forwards them. Both variables interpolate unquoted, so keep values free of *, ? and [].

docs.title: Backups (as kendo)
docs.text:
Nightly backup to ~/backups, keeping the newest 14 of each artefact, driven by a systemd user timer. Each run writes two files sharing one timestamp:

File Contents kendo-<stamp>.dump Postgres, pg_dump custom format kendo-uploads-<stamp>.tar the kendo-app-uploads volume — logos and login backgrounds

Uploaded images live on a volume, not in the database, so the dump alone does not cover them.

cp deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.service ~/.config/systemd/user/
cp deploy/systemd/kendo-backup.timer   ~/.config/systemd/user/
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now kendo-backup.timer

# Verify schedule + run once now
systemctl --user list-timers kendo-backup.timer --no-pager
systemctl --user start kendo-backup.service
ls -lh ~/backups

Restore (destructive — stops writes, drops/recreates the DB):

systemctl --user stop kendo-app
# Second argument is optional; pass the uploads tarball with the same timestamp
# to restore logos and backgrounds alongside the database.
~/.local/bin/kendo-restore.sh \
  ~/backups/kendo-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.dump \
  ~/backups/kendo-uploads-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.tar
systemctl --user start kendo-app

Copy backups off-box. A dump on the same host does not survive host loss. Ship ~/backups elsewhere (rsync/restic/object storage) — not implemented here.

docs.title: Quick self-host
docs.text:
This is a supported production path for a single dojo: one host, Traefik terminating TLS with a Let's Encrypt certificate, three commands.

Outgrowing it? The Hardened deployment is what you graduate to — the same setup.sh, run as ./setup.sh --quadlet, adds systemd units, Podman secrets, network segmentation and automated backups.

1. Get the deployment files:

The release image carries the files a deployment needs — this compose file, the .example config, the Quadlet units, the backup scripts and setup.sh — so there is no clone and no build (ADR-0004):

podman run --rm ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:1 init | tar -x

(Working from a checkout instead? Skip that — the files are already here.)

2. Configure it:

./setup.sh

It asks for your domain and an ACME email, generates POSTGRES_PASSWORD, JWT_SECRET and SETUP_TOKEN, and writes .env plus deploy/traefik/selfhost/traefik.yml and dynamic/kendo.yml from their .example files. One domain answer reaches all three passkey-bound settings (WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN, CORS_ORIGINS) and the Traefik Host() rule — an RP_ID typo is the whole "passkeys silently don't work" failure class, so it is worth not typing four times.

TLS is one question with four answers: Let's Encrypt production, Let's Encrypt staging (rehearse a new domain without burning the production rate limit), bring your own certificate, or skip. Orthogonally, the ACME challenge is HTTP-01 (default, needs inbound 80), TLS-ALPN-01 (needs inbound 443 only — the answer when an ISP blocks 80) or DNS-01 (no inbound ports; it prompts for your lego provider slug and prints the credentials that provider wants).

Re-running is safe: existing secrets are carried forward rather than regenerated, and any file it rewrites is kept as .bak. The written files are gitignored, so upgrading cannot revert your domain or email to the shipped placeholders. Prefer doing it by hand? Every file it writes has a documented .example next to it.

The script also checks the five host prerequisites — Podman, the net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=80 sysctl rootless Podman needs to bind 80/443, the firewall, the kendo user and loginctl enable-linger — and prints the exact sudo command for each one that is missing. It never escalates itself; you run those.

3. Check, then start the stack:

./setup.sh check       # green? then:
podman-compose up -d   # pulls ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:1

check looks at what the app cannot see from inside its container, the things that otherwise surface as a browser error or a certificate that never arrives: placeholder domains, emails or secrets left in .env or the Traefik files, a Traefik Host() rule that no longer matches WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, TLS skipped or a bring-your-own certificate not in place, the domain not resolving to this host, something else already on 80/443, and the five host prerequisites. Each FAIL names its fix; it changes nothing and exits non-zero on any FAIL. A warn is something it cannot decide from here — DNS pointing at a router's public address is right behind NAT — and does not fail it. Run it any time: after an upgrade, after a domain change, or paste its output into a bug report.

KENDO_IMAGE in .env is the pin. The documented default is the major tag :1: fixes and features, but no migration that needs a restore from backup to undo. Moving to :2 is a deliberate edit, made after reading the release notes.

Contributors still build from source — make build produces localhost/kendodojo:latest; set KENDO_IMAGE=localhost/kendodojo:latest to run it.

Traefik serves the app on 443 and redirects 80 to it. The app service publishes no host port of its own: every request arrives through the proxy, which is what makes TRUST_PROXY_XFF (on by default here) safe — Traefik overwrites X-Forwarded-For with the address it observed, so rate limiting and account lockout see a client IP the client cannot choose. If you re-publish the app's port, set TRUST_PROXY_XFF=false in the same edit.

Alembic migrations run in the migrate service, which runs alembic upgrade head and exits; app starts only once it has succeeded. Uploaded logos and backgrounds persist in the static_uploads named volume, and the database in postgres_data — both survive down/up and image rebuilds.

docs.title: Quick self-host (Compose)
docs.text:
./setup.sh upgrade

An upgrade runs alembic upgrade head against your live database, so this takes a backup first: deploy/bin/kendo-backup.sh writes the database dump and the uploads tarball to ~/backups and says where. Then it pulls, refreshes the deployment bundle from the image it just pulled, and recreates the stack. The bundle holds the compose file, the .example config and the Quadlet units, so they always match the app they run. Any of those files that changed is listed, and your previous copy is kept as .bak. .env and your filled-in Traefik files are never touched.

A file you edited yourself (a BYO certificate's mount in docker-compose.yml, say) is never overwritten. If this release also changed it, the new version is written next to it as .new and the upgrade stops before anything is recreated. Merge the two, re-run ./setup.sh upgrade, and it carries on.

If the upgrade or the migration fails, it prints the exact kendo-restore.sh command for the backup it just took. It also prints the digest of the image that was running, to pin back to. Restoring the data alone is only half a rollback, because the new image would migrate it straight back up.

Some migrations check your data before changing the schema, and stop if they find rows only you can decide about — for example an account that belongs to no member, or a member whose email differs from the account that signs in as them (#432). They stop before changing anything, name the rows, and say what to fix. Fix those rows, then run ./setup.sh upgrade again.

A plain podman-compose pull && podman-compose up -d is not enough on Podman: podman-compose recreates a container only when the compose file changes, so a new image under the same :1 tag never starts.

Upgrading a Compose stack first started before #385: the image now runs as the unprivileged user kendo (uid 1001), but Podman only takes a volume's ownership from the image when the volume is empty, so a static_uploads created by the old root-running image stays root-owned and the first upload after the upgrade fails with a permission error. Chown it once:

# Compose prefixes the volume with the project name — find it first:
vol=$(podman volume ls --format '{{.Name}}' | grep static_uploads)
podman unshare chown -R 1001:1001 \
  "$(podman volume inspect "$vol" --format '{{.Mountpoint}}')"

The Quadlet path needs no such step — kendo-app.container mounts the volume with :U, which chowns it on every start. Fresh stacks need nothing either.

docs.title: Hardened deployment (Quadlet)
docs.text:
When a Quadlet unit, the Traefik config or the env file changes upstream, the Upgrade command above is not enough — it pulls the image but reuses the units already in ~/.config/containers/systemd/, the Traefik config already in ~/kendo/traefik/, and it never touches ~/kendo/kendo-app.env. Each is a copy made once at install time; pulling a new image updates neither.

# Re-extract the bundle from the tag you are pinned to — it ships inside the
# image, so the units below match the app they start.
cd ~/src && podman run --rm ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:1 init | tar -x

# Units: re-run the copy from Hardened deployment §2-4, then daemon-reload so Quadlet regenerates.
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.network   ~/.config/containers/systemd/
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.volume    ~/.config/containers/systemd/
cp deploy/quadlet/kendo-*.container ~/.config/containers/systemd/
systemctl --user daemon-reload

# Traefik dynamic config — keep your Host() rule, take the rest. Traefik
# watches this directory, so no restart is needed once the file lands.
diff deploy/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml ~/kendo/traefik/dynamic/kendo.yml

systemctl --user restart kendo-migrate kendo-app

The env file is per-host and needs comparing rather than copying — see Refreshing the env file.

A host installed before #412 that uses DNS-01 needs the drop-in before its next unit refresh. kendo-traefik.container used to hardcode CF_DNS_API_TOKEN_FILE and the kendo_cf_dns_token secret; it no longer does, so re-copying it leaves Traefik with no DNS credentials and ACME renewal fails. Write the drop-in from §5 first — pointing Secret= at your existing kendo_cf_dns_token is fine, no new secret needed.

Hosts installed before #385 need the unit refresh now. That change made the app run unprivileged and mounts the uploads volume :U; both live in kendo-app.container, so neither reaches an existing host until the copy above. The edge health check lives in the Traefik dynamic config.

docs.title: Refreshing the env file after an upgrade
docs.text:
Re-extracting the bundle updates deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example in ~/src. It does not update ~/kendo/kendo-app.env — that file is yours, per host, and nothing overwrites it except a deliberate re-run of ./setup.sh --quadlet, which rewrites it from the example (keeping the previous one as kendo-app.env.bak). That is the quickest way to pick up new keys, and it discards any local edit beyond the three domain values, so compare the two afterwards if you have any. When an upgrade adds a setting, the app silently runs without it: the Quadlet unit passes this one EnvironmentFile and nothing else, so a key absent from it is absent from the app's environment.

Compare keys, not lines. Values legitimately differ per host, so a plain diff is all noise; the keys are what drift:

diff <(grep -oE '^[A-Z0-9_]+=' ~/kendo/kendo-app.env | tr -d = | sort) \
     <(grep -oE '^[A-Z0-9_]+=' ~/src/deploy/env/kendo-app.env.example | tr -d = | sort)

Empty output means nothing new upstream. A > line is a setting you are missing — copy it across with its comment, then restart:

systemctl --user restart kendo-app

A changed EnvironmentFile needs only a restart; a changed unit file needs re-copying and a daemon-reload first — the note under the table above has that sequence.

Then verify the app actually received it — a restart proves the unit started, not that the value arrived:

podman exec kendo-app printenv APP_ENV JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES
# APP_ENV=production
# JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES=480

Hosts deployed before #386 need this now. That change added APP_ENV=production (without it the app takes its development path and skips every production WebAuthn check at startup) and raised JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES to 480. Both live in the env file, so neither reaches an existing host until you copy them across.

docs.title: 387 adds SESSION_MAX_MINUTES (default 10080 — 7 days), the ceiling on a
docs.text: session that sliding renewal keeps alive. It defaults in app/config.py, so an existing host needs it in the env file only to override that default.

docs.title: Upgrading a deployment created before the Alembic baseline (issue #264)
docs.text:
As of issue #264, the Alembic chain has a baseline migration (000000000000) that creates the full schema from nothing, so alembic upgrade head now works against a genuinely empty database. This changes nothing for an instance that was already deployed and running:

  • Any instance deployed before this change already has an alembic_version row naming a revision at or after a1b2c3d4e5f6 (every prior deploy got its schema from Base.metadata.create_all followed by alembic stamp head on first boot). Alembic walks forward from whatever revision is recorded in alembic_version; it does not replay or re-verify ancestors behind that revision. The new baseline is an ancestor of a1b2c3d4e5f6 and is simply never visited. alembic upgrade head continues to work exactly as before — no action needed.
  • A legacy pre-Alembic instance (tables exist, but there is no alembic_version table at all — only possible if the instance predates a1b2c3d4e5f6 merging and has never restarted since; every restart under the pre-#264 bootstrap already ran alembic upgrade head unconditionally for a non-empty database, which creates alembic_version on its first successful migration) needs one manual step before its next alembic upgrade head:
podman exec kendo-app alembic stamp head

This is correct only if you're confident the instance's schema matches the current ORM exactly (i.e. it's been kept current) — the same assumption the pre-#264 bootstrap made for a "fresh" database (create_all then stamp head), and safe for the same reason: test_migrated_schema_matches_orm_metadata_exactly guarantees a create_all schema and a fully-migrated schema are identical at head. Do not stamp at a1b2c3d4e5f6 or at the new baseline (000000000000) — either leaves alembic_version naming a revision before tables this instance's create_all already built (federations, member_federations, invites, and everything added after them), so the next alembic upgrade head tries to create things that already exist and fails.

If there's any doubt the schema is current — the instance predates some migration that shipped after it was last redeployed — no single stamp target is correct, and guessing one will silently leave the database wrong (either missing real schema changes, or erroring out trying to redo ones it already has). Diff the live schema against app.db.base.Base.metadata first (e.g. via alembic.autogenerate.compare_metadata, the same check test_migrated_schema_matches_orm_metadata_exactly runs) to see exactly what's missing, then either apply those changes by hand and stamp head, or — safer — back up the data, run alembic upgrade head against a fresh empty database, and migrate the data across instead of reconciling the old schema in place. See the baseline migration's docstring (backend/alembic/versions/000000000000_baseline_schema.py) for the full reasoning.

docs.title: Break-glass recovery
docs.text:
Use this when the only admin is locked out and has no recovery codes.

podman exec kendo-app python -m app.cli create-recovery-token <email>

This prints a single-use plaintext token valid for 60 minutes. Redeem it at:

  • API: POST /auth/recovery/redeem — body {"email": "<email>", "code": "<token>"}
  • Login page: enter the email and paste the token into the recovery code field

Security notes: - Run this command on the server only — never over an untrusted network. - The token is stored as a bcrypt hash; the plaintext is never persisted. - Delete the token from your terminal history after use.

docs.title: Claim the admin account (the setup token gates it)
docs.text:
On the quick self-host the token is SETUP_TOKEN in .env, and the commands below that name kendo-app or a podman secret are the Quadlet spellings: the claim itself is the same request either way.

The instance is now reachable. Claiming the first admin account requires the kendo_setup_token secret from section 2-4 — the setup endpoints answer 401 {"detail": "Invalid setup token"} without it (ADR-0003). Nothing to race: an opportunistic scanner that finds the host minutes after Traefik's Let's Encrypt certificate hits the certificate transparency logs cannot claim anything without that value.

The token is required whether or not the instance is already claimed: the app refuses to start without it, so do not delete the secret after claiming. A database restore or wipe would otherwise boot an unclaimed instance with no gate in front of it.

The browser is the way you do this. Open https://<your-domain>/: the setup page asks for the admin's first name, surname and email, and the setup token. The claim creates the admin's member record as well as their account — every account belongs to a member, the first admin included — and the email is the one they will sign in with. Paste the token into the "Setup token" field and complete the passkey registration. The page sends it as an X-Setup-Token header on /api/setup/passkey/begin and /api/setup/passkey/complete, and a wrong token comes back on the form as "Invalid setup token". The value is never stored in the browser — reloading the page means pasting it again.

No shell access is needed to claim the account, so the URL and the token can go to whoever is becoming the admin. The curl below is for debugging a claim that is not working, not a step:

curl -sS -X POST https://<your-domain>/api/setup/passkey/begin \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "X-Setup-Token: $SETUP_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"email":"admin@your-dojo","first_name":"Ai","surname":"Sato"}'
# 401 {"detail":"Invalid setup token"} -> wrong or missing token.
# 404 {"detail":"Setup already completed"} -> claimed; the token is irrelevant.

Then confirm the window is shut.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<your-domain>/api/setup
# 404 -> setup is closed, an account exists.
# 200 -> still unclaimed (the token is still required to claim it).
# anything else (000, 502, ...) -> the check never reached the app. That is not
# a closed window; fix the request and re-run before you believe it.

The claimed guard counts passkey credentials, not users: an abandoned ceremony leaves a user row with no credential and deliberately does not count, so an operator whose browser died mid-ceremony is never locked out.

Lost the token? Rotate it — nothing in the database has to change:

# Keep the value: a podman secret cannot be read back, so piping straight into
# `secret create` leaves you with a token nobody knows.
token=$(openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n')
podman secret rm kendo_setup_token
printf '%s' "$token" | podman secret create kendo_setup_token -
systemctl --user restart kendo-app
echo "$token"   # hand it over out of band, then clear your scrollback

app/cli.py create-recovery-token does not cover a never-claimed instance: it resolves a User row by email, and an unclaimed instance has none. Rotation is the only path there, and it costs seconds.

docs.title: Day-2 operations
docs.text:
Task Command (as kendo via machinectl shell kendo@) Status systemctl --user status kendo-app --no-pager Logs podman logs -f kendo-app Restart app systemctl --user restart kendo-app Upgrade — the full procedure is Upgrading podman pull ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:1 && systemctl --user restart kendo-migrate kendo-app Stop all systemctl --user stop kendo-traefik kendo-app kendo-migrate kendo-db Break-glass recovery podman exec kendo-app python -m app.cli create-recovery-token <email>

The pin is the Image= line in the two Quadlet units, and the documented value is the major tag :1 — fixes and features, but no migration that needs a restore from backup to undo. Moving to :2 is a deliberate edit made after reading the release notes. Building from source still works (podman build -t localhost/kendodojo:latest .); point Image= at it.

docs.title: Container architecture
docs.text:
File Purpose Dockerfile Multi-stage build: backend-deps → backend-dev-deps → frontend-deps → frontend-build → prod docker-compose.yml Production stack (app + PostgreSQL, named volumes for db data and uploads) docker-compose.dev.yml Dev stack with bind-mounted source and hot-reload docker-compose.test.yml Test watcher stack with ephemeral PostgreSQL .env.example Template for production secrets .env.dev Dev defaults (safe to commit) .env.test Test defaults (safe to commit)

Each stack sets an explicit Compose project name — kendodojo, kendodojo-dev and kendodojo-test. Without it Compose derives the name from the directory, so all three resolved to the same containers, networks and volumes: starting the dev database silently replaced the test one, and down on either file removed containers belonging to the other.

If you have a checkout from before this change, your old containers and volumes are still named after the directory (kendodojomanagement_*) and are now orphaned. To carry dev data across:

podman exec kendodojomanagement_db_1 pg_dump -U kendo_dev -d kendo_dev > dev.sql
podman rm -f kendodojomanagement_db_1
podman-compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file .env.dev up -d db
podman exec -i kendodojo-dev_db_1 psql -U kendo_dev -d kendo_dev < dev.sql
podman volume rm kendodojomanagement_postgres_dev_data   # once you are happy

Nothing needs carrying across for the test stack — its database is deliberately volume-less and is rebuilt on every run.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: The two env templates are the reference: every variable is documented in place, next to the value it ships with. They are included here as they are in the release you are reading.

docs.title: Quick self-host — .env
docs.text:
./setup.sh writes .env from this template, filling in the domain and generating the three secrets.

# Template for the production Compose stack (docker-compose.yml).
# Start it with: podman-compose --env-file .env up -d
# Copy to .env and fill in real values — .env is gitignored, never commit it.

# The image docker-compose.yml runs, for `app` and `migrate` alike. The
# documented pin is the MAJOR tag (ADR-0004): `:1` takes fixes and features but
# no migration that needs a restore from backup to undo; `./setup.sh upgrade`
# backs up, pulls and migrates. Move to `:2` deliberately, after reading the
# release notes. `:1.4`, `:1.4.0` and `:latest` are also published; a contributor
# running their own build sets this to localhost/kendodojo:latest.
KENDO_IMAGE=ghcr.io/booji/kendodojomanagement:1

# Container timezone (IANA name). Applies to app and db.
TZ=UTC

# development | production. docker-compose.yml already defaults this to
# production; set it here only to override. On production the app refuses to
# start while WEBAUTHN_RP_ID / WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN are still at their localhost
# dev defaults.
APP_ENV=production

# Required — the app refuses to start if this is unset/blank.
DATABASE_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://kendo:<your-db-password>@db:5432/kendo
POSTGRES_USER=kendo
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<your-db-password>
POSTGRES_DB=kendo
# Required — the app refuses to start if this is unset/blank.
# Generate with: python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))"
JWT_SECRET=<your-jwt-secret>
# Required — the app refuses to start if this is unset/blank, claimed or not.
# Whoever holds it can claim the first admin account on an unclaimed instance,
# so treat it like a password and hand it over out of band.
# Generate with: openssl rand -base64 32
SETUP_TOKEN=<your-setup-token>
# Token lifetime, and so the idle timeout. A session in use slides: any
# authenticated request past half the token's life re-issues the cookie (#387),
# so this is a gap of inactivity rather than a cut-off mid-work. Renewal only
# fires in the second half of a token's life, so the idle window a user sees is
# between half this value and all of it (4-8 hours at 480), depending on when
# their last request fell. 480 matches the default in app/config.py.
JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES=480
# The ceiling on one session however continuously it is used: past it the
# cookie expires and the user signs in again. Without it sliding renewal means
# "signed in forever". 10080 = 7 days, matching app/config.py.
SESSION_MAX_MINUTES=10080
# Set to false only for local dev (localhost does not support Secure cookies)
COOKIE_SECURE=true

# Public domain the browser uses. Passkeys are bound to these values: RP_ID is
# the bare host (no scheme, no port), ORIGIN is the full origin. Getting them
# wrong makes every passkey ceremony fail.
WEBAUTHN_RP_ID=<your-domain.com>
WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN=https://<your-domain.com>
WEBAUTHN_CHALLENGE_TTL_SECONDS=300

# Comma-separated allowed CORS origins. Keep pinned to the canonical origin —
# never "*", auth is cookie-based. Defaults to WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN if left empty.
CORS_ORIGINS=https://<your-domain.com>

# Minimum wall-clock time (ms) the passkey begin endpoints take, regardless of
# whether the email is known/registered or not. Prevents timing-based email
# enumeration, and only works while the real path finishes underneath it.
# 100ms is measured, not guessed: the real path's p99 against PostgreSQL is
# 16.8ms and its worst observed case 27.9ms, with headroom for slower
# production storage. See docs/auth-timing-calibration.md before changing it.
AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS=100

# Read the client IP from X-Forwarded-For (used by rate limiting and account
# lockout). docker-compose.yml defaults this to true, which is safe there and
# only there: Traefik fronts the app, and the app publishes no host port of its
# own, so the header cannot arrive from a client. Left false here because .env
# is also what a hand-rolled run outside that compose file uses — with nothing
# overwriting the header, a client picks its own IP and gets a fresh
# rate-limit and lockout bucket per request.
TRUST_PROXY_XFF=false

# Upload paths are set in docker-compose.yml and backed by the static_uploads
# volume; do not override STATIC_DIR / STATIC_BACKGROUNDS_DIR here or uploads
# will be written outside the volume and lost on restart.

docs.title: Hardened deployment — ~/kendo/kendo-app.env
docs.text:
Non-sensitive settings only. DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET and SETUP_TOKEN are podman secrets under the hardened deployment, not variables in this file — see Hardened deployment.

# Non-sensitive app config for UAT/PROD. Copy to ~kendo/kendo/kendo-app.env and
# edit the domain values. Secrets (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET) are NOT here — they
# are podman secrets injected by the Quadlet unit.
#
# Per-host file: UAT and PROD differ ONLY in the domain-derived values below.

# Selects the production config path in app/config.py: with this unset the app
# falls back to "development" and skips every WebAuthn RP ID / origin shape
# check in validate_startup_config(), so a placeholder domain or an http://
# origin boots cleanly and only fails in the browser (#385). The Quadlet unit
# passes this file and nothing else, so it has to be set here.
APP_ENV=production

# Container timezone (IANA name). Sets local time for the app; keep the db
# (deploy/quadlet/kendo-db.container) in sync. Defaults to UTC if unset.
TZ=Europe/London

# Public domain (no scheme, no port) — must match the Traefik Host() rule.
WEBAUTHN_RP_ID=dojo.example.com
WEBAUTHN_ORIGIN=https://dojo.example.com

# Same-origin SPA, so CORS is effectively inert — but keep it pinned to the one
# canonical origin (never "*"). Fails closed if a cross-origin path ever appears.
CORS_ORIGINS=https://dojo.example.com

# TLS terminates at Traefik; cookies must still be Secure.
COOKIE_SECURE=true

# Trust X-Forwarded-For for client IP (rate limiting). MUST be true
# here because the app sits behind Traefik; leaving it false collapses per-client
# limits into one global bucket. Safe: the app publishes no ports and is only
# reachable via Traefik, which overwrites the header.
TRUST_PROXY_XFF=true

# Token lifetime, and so the idle timeout. A session in active use slides: any
# authenticated request past half the token's life re-issues the cookie,
# re-reading the user row as it does (#387), so this is a gap of inactivity
# rather than a cut-off mid-work, and an expiry now lands the user on the login
# page rather than on "Not authorized" toasts. Renewal only fires in the second
# half of a token's life, so the idle window a user sees is between half this
# value and all of it (4-8 hours at 480). 480 matches app/config.py.
JWT_EXPIRE_MINUTES=480
# The ceiling on one session however continuously it is used: past it the
# cookie expires and the user signs in again (one passkey touch). Without it,
# sliding renewal means "signed in forever". 10080 = 7 days.
SESSION_MAX_MINUTES=10080
WEBAUTHN_CHALLENGE_TTL_SECONDS=300
# Minimum wall-clock time (ms) the passkey begin endpoints take, regardless of
# whether the email is known/registered or not. Prevents timing-based email
# enumeration; it only masks anything while the real path (commit+fsync
# included) finishes underneath it. 100ms is measured against PostgreSQL, not
# guessed: real-path p99 16.8ms, worst observed 27.9ms, the rest headroom for
# slower storage than the box it was measured on. Alert on the app log's
# "Constant-time floor exceeded" warning — that is the signal this floor has
# stopped protecting anything. See docs/auth-timing-calibration.md.
AUTH_BEGIN_MIN_DURATION_MS=100

# Upload targets. These MUST stay under /app/uploads — that is where the
# kendo-app-uploads volume is mounted, and anything written outside it is lost
# on restart. Kept out of /app/static too, which holds the built SPA.
STATIC_DIR=/app/uploads/logos
STATIC_BACKGROUNDS_DIR=/app/uploads/backgrounds

Not a person — it always belongs to exactly one Member, and signs in with that Member's email. The code still calls it User / users until the rename lands (#436) User, login Role The permission level of an Account: either admin or member Permission, access level Passkey A WebAuthn credential stored on a device, used for passwordless authentication Biometric login, FIDO key First-registered Admin The first Member to register on a fresh instance: their Member and Account are created together when they claim it, with the admin Role Superuser, root user

docs.text: Term Definition Aliases to avoid User Settings Per-user configuration accessible to every authenticated user: Personal Details and Appearance Settings (unqualified when dojo settings are also in scope) Personal Details The subset of Member fields a Member can edit themselves: name, DOB, emergency contact, federation number Profile settings Appearance The User Settings section controlling visual preferences, specifically the Theme Display settings Theme A Member's preferred colour scheme: light, dark, or system (follows device preference) Dark mode, colour scheme Dojo Settings Admin-managed configuration scoped to the whole instance: name, primary colour, logo Settings (unqualified when user settings are also in scope)

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Every Account belongs to exactly one Member; a Member has at most one Account. There is no sign-in without a kendoka behind it.
  • An Account has exactly one Role: admin or member.
  • Only an Admin can change a Member's email: the app sends no mail, so a self-service change could not be verified.
  • A Member holds exactly one current Grade and accumulates a Grade History over time.
  • A Grade progresses in strict order: Mukyū → 6-kyū → 5-kyū → 4-kyū → 3-kyū → 2-kyū → 1-kyū → 1-dan → 2-dan → 3-dan → 4-dan → 5-dan → 6-dan → 7-dan → 8-dan.
  • A Session is either generated from a Session Template or created as an Ad-hoc Session.
  • A Session has one or more Segments, and each Segment carries one or more Session Types — so a single evening keiko can be both Kihon and Keiko.
  • Attendance at a Session is a collection of Check-ins by Members and named Visitors.
  • A Session has exactly one Check-in Link, and it never changes.
  • A Minor requires a Parental Consent flag before being considered fully registered.
  • A Deactivation sets Membership Status to inactive; it never removes the Member or their Account.
  • A Member may hold a Federation Membership with each of several Federations; an Admin manages any member's, a Member manages their own, and both go through the same card.

These are environment names rather than domain concepts, but they are used constantly in discussion and "production" was ambiguous between two different stacks, so they are pinned here.

docs.title: Example dialogue
docs.text:
Dev: "When an admin 'deletes' a member, what happens to their account?"

Domain expert: "There is no deletion — the operation is a Deactivation. The Member stays in the database with Membership Status set to inactive. Their Account is also retained so they could be reactivated later."

Dev: "And what's the difference between the Account and the Member?"

Domain expert: "The Member is the kendoka: name, email, grade, emergency contact. The Account is just how they sign in: passkeys and a Role. Every Account belongs to a Member, but most Members on the roster never sign in, so they have none."

Dev: "If I'm building the settings page, should I call it 'User Settings' or just 'Settings'?"

Domain expert: "Call it User Settings whenever Dojo Settings might also be in scope. Unqualified 'settings' is ambiguous — User Settings covers personal details and appearance; Dojo Settings covers dojo-wide configuration like name and colours."

Dev: "What Theme does a new member see?"

Domain expert: "System — the device preference is the default. The member can override it to light or dark in Appearance, and that choice is saved to their account so it follows them across devices."

Dev: "When we record a Promotion, who is the awarder?"

Domain expert: "The Admin who performs the promotion. It's stored in the Grade History alongside the date, so there's always an audit trail of who awarded each Grade."

docs.title: Flagged ambiguities
docs.text:
• "User": Retired as a domain term (#418) because it sounds like a person, and the person is always the Member. The sign-in is the Account. "The user's name" means "the Member's name"; there is no such thing as a user's email, only the Member's. The code keeps User until the rename lands (#436). User Settings stays as a page name.
  • "Settings": Used unqualified for both per-user preferences and dojo-wide configuration. Always qualify: User Settings or Dojo Settings.
  • "Delete" vs "Deactivate": The API endpoint DELETE /members/{id} performs a Deactivation, not a deletion. The word "delete" must not be used for this operation in any user-facing text, documentation, or domain discussion.
  • "Profile": Used loosely to mean the auth account, the member record, or both. The canonical term for the dojo record is Member. Avoid bare "profile" and the retired "Member Profile".
  • "Grading": Used in two senses — the event type (a session where grades are awarded) and the act of awarding a grade. Use Session Type: Grading for the event and Promotion for the act.
  • "Guest" and "Visitor": Used interchangeably in early discussion. The canonical term is Visitor.
  • "Rank" and "Grade": The canonical term is Grade, to align with kendo federation terminology.
  • "Production": Meant two different stacks — the Quadlet units in deploy/quadlet and the Compose file in docker-compose.yml. Both are supported production paths, so never use "production" to tell them apart: say quick self-host or hardened deployment.
